message.content:
The number of distinct legal positions that can arise in a standard game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated this number – now called the **Shannon number** – to be on the order of

\[
N_{\text{positions}} \;\approx\; 10^{43}
\]

(roughly 100 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000).

More recent computational studies have refined the estimate of the *exact* count of legal positions to be about \(10^{46}\), but the Shannon number remains the most widely cited figure because it captures the sheer scale of the combinatorial explosion in chess.

So, in short: there are roughly **10⁴³** possible legal arrangements of pieces on a chessboard.
